transcript.text: Productivity Measurement
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-11
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate output per worker and interpret productivity changes.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Labor productivity measures output per worker or per hour worked. For example, 2,400 units produced in 300 labor hours means 2,400 / 300 = 8 units per hour. Productivity compares output with the labor input used to produce it, so changes in both output and labor matter. A country can consume more when its workers produce more output per worker.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Measure labor productivity as real output per worker or per hour worked.
Use the same output and labor units when comparing periods.
An increase in total output need not raise productivity if labor input also rises.
WATCH OUT
Do not confuse total output with output per unit of labor. Productivity compares output with the labor input used to produce it, so changes in both output and labor matter.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MEASURING LABOR PRODUCTIVITY

A workshop produces 2,400 units using 300 labor hours, so productivity is 2,400 / 300 = 8 units per hour. Next month it produces 2,700 units using the same 300 hours: 9 units per hour. Productivity rises by (9 - 8) / 8 x 100 = 12.5%. More output per labor hour, not simply more total hours, is the improvement.
CHECK YOURSELF
A business uses more labor hours but produces the same amount of output. What happens to labor productivity?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Economic Growth Policy
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-13
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Evaluate policies affecting long-run productivity and growth.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Long-run growth policy raises productive capacity rather than current spending alone. Saving and reliable finance support capital formation; education builds human capital; research and competition can advance technology. Stable property rights and institutions make firms more willing to invest. Because physical capital faces diminishing returns, sustained growth usually depends on several of these channels working together.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The policy changes capital formation, human capital, technology, or institutions.
The question distinguishes productive capacity from a temporary demand increase.
Reliable finance and property rights affect whether saving becomes productive investment.
The proposed change can raise output per worker over time.
WATCH OUT

Do not treat a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity. Long-run growth policy works through productivity, capital formation, human capital, technology, and institutions.
WORKED EXAMPLE: EVALUATING A GROWTH POLICY

A government compares a temporary shopping rebate with worker training and reliable electricity for firms. The rebate can raise current spending, but training can improve skills and reliable power can reduce lost production. For long-run growth, evaluate the latter policies by their likely productivity gains, resource costs, implementation quality, and time to deliver results.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why might worker training raise long-run productive capacity while a temporary shopping rebate mainly changes current demand?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Labor-Market Institutions
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-16
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze minimum wages, unions, job search, and efficiency wages.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Labor-market institutions change wages, hiring, search incentives, and the balance between labor supplied and labor demanded. Efficiency wages can improve effort and reduce turnover. A binding minimum wage can create a surplus of labor, meaning more workers want jobs than firms want to hire. Unemployment insurance can support job seekers, but may also reduce urgency to accept a job quickly.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A binding minimum wage can create a surplus of labor, meaning more workers want jobs than firms want to hire.
Unemployment insurance can support job seekers, but may also reduce urgency to accept a job quickly.
A firm raises wages above equilibrium and worker effort rises enough to improve productivity, but fewer workers are hired at the higher wage.
Unemployment insurance can reduce the cost of continued job search, which may lengthen unemployment spells.
Union wage bargaining can raise wages above equilibrium and reduce the quantity of labor demanded.
WATCH OUT

Do not forget that a binding wage floor creates a surplus when labor supplied exceeds labor demanded. A binding minimum wage can create a surplus of labor, meaning more workers want jobs than firms want to hire.
WORKED EXAMPLE: BINDING MINIMUM WAGE

Wage per hour vertical, quantity of labor in workers horizontal. Labor supply slopes up and demand down, meeting at wage 12 and 105 workers. A binding minimum wage of 15 is above equilibrium. At that wage QD is 90 and QS is 120; a bracket marks a labor surplus of 30 workers.

At a binding minimum wage, 120 workers want jobs and firms hire 90. The labor surplus is 120 - 90 = 30 workers. The wage is held above equilibrium, so the quantity of labor supplied exceeds the quantity demanded.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why can more generous unemployment insurance lengthen some unemployment spells even while protecting workers?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-20
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Classify bank accounts and trace how transactions change reserves and capital.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A bank balance sheet satisfies assets = liabilities + capital. Reserves, loans, and securities are assets. Deposits and bank borrowing are liabilities. Bank capital is owners' equity: assets minus liabilities. Reserves provide liquidity and help meet withdrawals; capital absorbs asset losses. Required reserves and capital requirements therefore constrain different parts of the balance sheet.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A customer's deposit is a bank liability; the cash or reserve balance received is an asset.
A cash withdrawal reduces both reserves and deposits by the same amount.
A loan is a bank asset because the borrower owes the bank repayment.
An asset loss reduces capital when liabilities do not change.
WATCH OUT
Do not call reserves bank capital. Reserves are assets available for payments; capital is the residual claim, assets minus liabilities, that cushions losses.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CAPITAL ABSORBS AN ASSET LOSS

Before the loss, assets equal liabilities plus capital: $1,000 = $940 + $60. A $25 loan loss reduces loans and total assets while liabilities are unchanged. Afterward, $975 = $940 + $35. Capital absorbs the loss; reserves remain $120.
CHECK YOURSELF
If a depositor withdraws $20 in cash, which asset and which liability fall?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Long-Run Phillips Curve
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-38
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Apply the natural-rate hypothesis and vertical long-run Phillips curve.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural unemployment rate because expected inflation eventually adjusts. A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate. Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate. The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.
Expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 5 percent while unemployment remains at its natural rate.
The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.
A national job-matching system reduces the time workers spend searching for suitable positions.
WATCH OUT

Do not treat a higher expected inflation rate as a permanent way to lower unemployment. Along the long-run Phillips curve, different inflation rates can coexist with the same natural rate of unemployment.
WORKED EXAMPLE: RETURNING TO THE NATURAL RATE

Unemployment horizontal, inflation vertical. LRPC is vertical at 5 percent unemployment. Initial A on SRPC0 is (5,3). Demand expansion moves along SRPC0 to B (3,5). Expected inflation adjustment shifts SRPC up to SRPC1; final C (5,5) is at its intersection with LRPC. Arrows show A to B to C.

The economy starts at A: 5% unemployment and 3% inflation. A demand expansion moves it along SRPC0 to B, at 3% unemployment and 5% inflation. As expected inflation rises, SRPC shifts up to SRPC1. The final point C is on LRPC at 5% unemployment and 5% inflation. Unemployment returns to its natural rate; there is no permanent inflation-unemployment tradeoff.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why does higher inflation not permanently lower unemployment in the natural-rate model?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Tax Wedges and Revenue
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-02
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate tax wedges, buyer and seller prices, quantity effects, and revenue.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A per-unit tax creates a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive. The wedge reduces the quantity traded because some exchanges whose benefits formerly exceeded their costs no longer occur. Tax revenue equals the per-unit wedge multiplied by the post-tax quantity, while the lost mutually beneficial trades create deadweight loss.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Identify the tax wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive.
Use the post-tax quantity, not the original equilibrium quantity, when measuring revenue.
Tax revenue equals the per-unit tax multiplied by the quantity traded after the tax.
A tax normally reduces quantity traded and creates deadweight loss from forgone exchanges.
WATCH OUT
Tax revenue equals the per-unit tax times the quantity actually traded after the tax. Use the $6 wedge and 80 units here; do not multiply by the original untaxed quantity.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING TAX REVENUE

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price in dollars. Demand slopes down. Supply slopes up, intersecting demand at quantity 100 and price 15. A parallel Supply + tax curve above supply intersects demand at quantity 80 and price 18. At quantity 80, original supply is at price 12. Dashed guides also mark prices 10 and 20 and quantities 65, 120 and 150.

The untaxed equilibrium is $15 at 100 units. After the tax, buyers pay $18, sellers receive $12, and quantity falls to 80. The tax wedge is $18 - $12 = $6 per unit, so government revenue is $6 x 80 = $480.
CHECK YOURSELF
Buyers pay $18 after a tax and sellers receive $12. What is the tax per unit?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Cross-Price Elasticity of Demand
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-07
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate Cross-Price Elasticity of Demand.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Cross-price elasticity measures how demand for one good responds to a price change in another good. A large positive cross-price coefficient signals a strong substitution relationship. Complementary goods connect through opposite movements between one price and the other good's demand. Demand for one good moving in the same direction as the other good’s price implies positive cross-price elasticity. Little demand response to the other good’s price implies little economic relationship between the goods.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The price of butter rises and demand for margarine rises.
Little demand response to the other good’s price implies little economic relationship between the goods.
Cross-price elasticity between printers and ink cartridges is -0.7.
A negative cross-price coefficient means demand moves opposite the other good’s price.
The price of Product Y falls 8 percent.
WATCH OUT
Do not confuse cross price with income or own price. A negative cross-price elasticity indicates complements, so higher printer prices reduce demand for ink.
WORKED EXAMPLE: IDENTIFYING COMPLEMENTS

The price of printers rises by 10%, and demand for ink cartridges falls by 7%. Cross-price elasticity is -7% / 10% = -0.7. The negative sign indicates that printers and ink cartridges are complements because a higher price for printers reduces demand for ink.
CHECK YOURSELF
Cross-price elasticity of ink demand with respect to printer price is -0.7. If printer price falls 5%, calculate the predicted percentage change in ink demand and state its direction.
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Changes in Surplus & Policy Effects
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-14
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Trace Changes in Surplus & Policy Effects.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A price or policy change can transfer surplus between buyers and sellers and can destroy surplus by preventing mutually beneficial trades. A transfer changes who receives existing gains without changing their total. Deadweight loss is different: it represents gains from exchange that disappear because quantity moves away from the efficient level.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Establish the initial consumer surplus, producer surplus, and total surplus before the change.
Recalculate those areas after the price change or policy intervention.
Separate transfers between buyers and sellers from surplus that disappears entirely.
Deadweight loss represents mutually beneficial trades prevented by the change.
WATCH OUT
A demand curve and price are enough to calculate consumer surplus. A change in consumer surplus alone does not establish the change in producer surplus, total surplus, or deadweight loss.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MEASURING A CHANGE IN CONSUMER SURPLUS

Demand slopes from price 20 at zero quantity to zero at 20. At price 12 quantity is 8 and the consumer-surplus triangle is 32. At price 8 quantity is 12 and the larger consumer-surplus triangle is 72. Distinct hatching marks these overlapping areas. No supply curve, producer surplus or deadweight loss is claimed.

At price P1 = $12, quantity is 8 and consumer surplus is 1/2 x 8 x ($20 - $12) = $32. At P2 = $8, quantity rises to 12 and consumer surplus becomes 1/2 x 12 x ($20 - $8) = $72. The price decrease raises consumer surplus by $40. These demand-side areas do not identify a transfer or deadweight loss without supply-side information.
CHECK YOURSELF
Consumer surplus rises from $32 to $72 after a price decrease. What is the gain, and can this information alone establish the change in total surplus?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Efficiency, Equity & Limits of Surplus Analysis
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-15
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish Efficiency, Equity & Limits of Surplus Analysis.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Efficiency concerns the size of total surplus, while equity concerns how benefits and costs are distributed. The efficiency result is positive analysis; deciding whether the distribution is fair adds a normative criterion. Surplus analysis compares value created with the opportunity cost of the resources used. Observed willingness to pay reflects both preferences and purchasing power. Efficiency and equity are different criteria; maximizing total gains does not determine how those gains are shared.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Use total surplus to evaluate efficiency and distributional evidence to evaluate equity.
Recognize that the allocation with the largest total surplus need not be the most equal.
Remember that measured willingness to pay depends partly on ability to pay.
A policy judgment requires an explicit value choice when efficiency and equity point in different directions.
WATCH OUT
Efficiency compares total gains; equity evaluates their distribution. Greater total surplus does not by itself establish that a policy is fair.
WORKED EXAMPLE: WEIGHING EFFICIENCY AND EQUITY

Policy A creates $500 of total surplus divided evenly between buyers and sellers. Policy B creates $520 of total surplus but gives $500 to sellers and $20 to buyers. Policy B is more efficient because total surplus is larger, but whether its distribution is more equitable is a separate normative judgment.
CHECK YOURSELF
A student says efficiency requires equal gains. Correction?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Domestic Production, Consumption & Trade Quantities
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-16
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Determine Domestic Production, Consumption & Trade Quantities.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

At a world price, domestic consumption is read from demand and domestic production is read from supply. When domestic consumption exceeds domestic production, imports fill the difference; when production exceeds consumption, the excess is exported. The comparison must be made at the world price because that price guides both domestic buyers and sellers under free trade.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Compare the world price with the domestic no-trade equilibrium price.
At the world price, read domestic consumption from demand and domestic production from supply.
When consumption exceeds production, imports equal domestic consumption minus domestic production.
When production exceeds consumption, exports equal domestic production minus domestic consumption.
WATCH OUT

When the world price exceeds the domestic no-trade equilibrium price, domestic supply exceeds domestic demand. The difference is exports, not imports. Do not infer tariff revenue or deadweight loss from this free-trade example.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING EXPORTS

Horizontal axis: quantity of avocados in thousands; vertical axis: price of avocados in dollars. Domestic demand slopes down and domestic supply slopes up. They intersect at A, quantity 175 thousand and price 7. A horizontal world-price line marked Pw = $10 meets demand at 100 thousand and supply at 250 thousand. Dashed vertical guides show those quantities.

Without trade, domestic supply and demand intersect at $7 and 175 thousand avocados. At the $10 world price, domestic consumers buy 100 thousand while domestic producers supply 250 thousand. The country exports the difference: 250 - 100 = 150 thousand avocados.
CHECK YOURSELF
Using the avocado export-market graph, what are domestic production, domestic consumption, and exports at Pw=$10?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Average Costs: AFC, AVC & ATC
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-22
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate Average Costs: AFC, AVC & ATC.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Average fixed cost, average variable cost, and average total cost express costs per unit of output. Average total cost equals average fixed cost plus average variable cost. Average fixed cost falls as output spreads the same fixed cost across more units, while average variable cost changes with the productivity and price of variable inputs.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Divide fixed cost by output for average fixed cost and variable cost by output for average variable cost.
Average total cost equals average fixed cost plus average variable cost.
Average fixed cost falls continuously as output spreads the same fixed cost across more units.
Use per-unit measures only when output is positive.
WATCH OUT
Average costs are per unit; total costs are not. Subtract AVC from ATC to find AFC, then multiply AFC by positive output to recover total fixed cost.
WORKED EXAMPLE: READING AVERAGE-COST CURVES

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: costs in dollars. Curves are labeled MC, AC and AVC. MC first dips slightly and then rises. It crosses AVC at its minimum, quantity 200 and cost 10. At quantity 400, MC crosses AC at its minimum of 20, while AVC is 12. Dashed guides mark the quantities and costs. AC remains above AVC.

At 400 units, the graph shows average cost of $20 and average variable cost of $12. Because AC = AVC + AFC, average fixed cost is $20 - $12 = $8 per unit. The gap between AC and AVC is therefore the firm's average fixed cost.
CHECK YOURSELF
At Q = 30, AVC is $14 and ATC is $24. Calculate AFC and total fixed cost. Verify your answer by multiplying the per-unit gap by output.
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Short-Run Supply & Cost Shifts
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-32
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze Short-Run Supply & Cost Shifts.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A competitive firm's short-run supply curve is the rising portion of marginal cost at and above minimum average variable cost. The tax is tied to each unit produced. MC gives the additional cost of supply. The short-run supply schedule depends on marginal and variable costs, not fixed cost.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Use the rising portion of marginal cost at and above minimum average variable cost as firm supply.
A variable-input cost increase shifts marginal cost and short-run supply upward or left.
A fixed-cost change shifts average total cost but leaves marginal cost and short-run supply unchanged.
Distinguish a movement along supply caused by price from a shift caused by production conditions.
WATCH OUT

Do not assume fixed cost shifts supply. The short-run supply schedule depends on marginal and variable costs, not fixed cost. Fixed cost affects profit but not the short-run MC-above-AVC supply schedule.
WORKED EXAMPLE: READING SHORT-RUN FIRM SUPPLY

Horizontal axis: firm quantity; vertical axis: cost / revenue. Horizontal P = MR = AR is at 10, below the entire AVC curve. MC crosses minimum AVC at A, quantity 22 and cost 20. Other marked points on rising MC are B near quantity 36 and cost 30, C near quantity 44 and cost 41 at minimum ATC, and D near quantity 50 and cost 50. Unprinted coordinates are approximate. ATC is above AVC.

The firm's short-run supply curve is the portion of MC at and above minimum AVC, which begins at point A: 22 units and $20. For example, if market price rises to $30, the firm supplies the quantity at point B, about 36 units. MC below A is not part of supply because the firm shuts down.
CHECK YOURSELF
Which MC segment is competitive short-run supply?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Oligopoly Structure, Strategic Interdependence & Concentration
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-48
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify Oligopoly Structure, Strategic Interdependence & Concentration.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

An oligopoly contains only a few important firms, so each firm's decisions depend on expected rival responses. Differentiation can exist in both; strategic few-firm response is distinctive. Dominant shares and strategic interdependence point to oligopoly. With only a few important firms, one firm’s action can provoke responses that change its own payoff.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for a market dominated by a few firms with meaningful barriers to entry.
Each firm's price, output, or advertising decision depends on how rivals are expected to respond.
Use concentration measures as evidence about structure, not as a complete verdict about competition.
The defining clue is strategic interdependence among the important firms.
WATCH OUT
Do not use firm count alone. Dominant shares and strategic interdependence point to oligopoly. Concentration depends on the boundaries of the relevant market.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MEASURING MARKET CONCENTRATION

Horizontal axis: Firm or fringe, with categories A, B, C, D and Other; vertical axis: Market share in percent. The five bars have printed values A 38 percent, B 32 percent, C 12 percent, D 9 percent, and Other 9 percent. Other is a separate aggregate category, not labeled as a single firm.

The named firms contribute 38^2 + 32^2 + 12^2 + 9^2 = 2,693 HHI points. The remaining 9% is labeled Other, an unspecified fringe. If it were one firm, it would add 9^2 = 81 points. Thus 2,774 is an upper bound, not an exact HHI. An exact calculation requires the individual fringe shares.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why can an aggregate Other category not generally be squared as if it were one firm when calculating exact HHI?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Dynamic Strategy: Repeated Games, Credibility & Entry Deterrence
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-51
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze repeated games, credible commitments, entry deterrence, and sequential strategic choices.
Difficulty: Advanced
THE CORE IDEA

In a sequential game, one player acts before another. Work backward from the last decision: identify the action that the later player will actually prefer, then use that response to evaluate the first move. A threat is credible only if carrying it out would be worthwhile when the decision arrives. Repeated interaction can make future consequences matter, but no present-value calculation is needed here.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Determine whether firms interact once or expect to meet again.
Compare the immediate gain from cheating or entering with future losses from retaliation.
A threat affects behavior only when carrying it out would be credible.
Longer relationships, patience, and observable actions make cooperative outcomes easier to sustain.
WATCH OUT
A threatened response is not automatically credible. Compare the later player's payoffs at the decision point before using the threat to predict the first move.
WORKED EXAMPLE: TESTING A CREDIBLE THREAT

Sequential game tree; payoffs are ordered Entrant, Incumbent. The Entrant moves first. Stay out ends with payoffs (0, 12). Enter leads to the Incumbent decision node. From that node, Accommodate ends with (6, 7), and Fight ends with (negative 3, 3). Branch labels identify the actions; each payoff belongs to its branch endpoint.

The game tree is solved backward. If entry occurs, the incumbent receives 7 by accommodating and 3 by fighting, so accommodation is the credible response on that branch. Anticipating it, the entrant compares 6 from entering with 0 from staying out and enters. The backward-induction outcome is Enter, then Accommodate.
CHECK YOURSELF
After entry, why will the incumbent accommodate rather than fight, and how does that affect the entrant's first decision?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Tacit Coordination, Price Leadership & Nonprice Competition
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-52
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze Tacit Coordination, Price Leadership & Nonprice Competition.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Tacit coordination occurs when firms align behavior without an explicit agreement, while nonprice competition uses quality, service, or advertising rather than price cuts. Advertising can shape demand in both markets. Strategic interdependence applies to quality, advertising, service, and other competitive dimensions as well as price. Tacit coordination refers to aligned behavior without the explicit agreement that defines collusion.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A student has learned that oligopoly firms react strategically to price changes.
A student says tacit coordination and explicit collusion are identical.
Tacit coordination can arise through expectations and repeated conduct.
A firm increases product quality rather than cutting price.
WATCH OUT
This is one simple model of price rigidity, not a claim that all oligopoly prices stay fixed. Firms can also compete through quality, service, and advertising.
WORKED EXAMPLE: AN INTRODUCTORY PRICE-RIGIDITY EXAMPLE

Quantity horizontal; price, cost and revenue vertical. Demand is flatter left of its kink at Q 20, P 50, and steeper right. Left demand is P = 60 minus 0.5 Q and right demand P = 80 minus 1.5 Q. MR branches end at 40 and start at 20 at Q 20. Horizontal MC 36 lies inside this downward MR gap. MR exceeds MC before the kink and is below MC after it.

Demand has a kink at Q = 20 and P = $50. Above that price, customers respond more strongly to a price increase; below it, rivals matching a cut limit the quantity gain. The corresponding MR gap runs from $20 to $40 at Q = 20. MC = $36 passes through that gap, so modest cost changes within it leave this model's chosen price and quantity unchanged.
CHECK YOURSELF
Does parallel pricing prove collusion?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
